title: Watch Venus Play Hide-and-Seek Behind the Moon!
summary: Have you ever seen a planet disappear? On June 17, you might get the chance! The Moon will pass directly in front of Venus, the brightest planet in our evening sky. This is called a lunar occultation (when one object in space hides another). For people in parts of the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Venezuela, Venus will seem to vanish behind the Moon and then reappear later. Even if you’re not in the perfect spot, the Moon and Venus will still look super close together. But wait, there’s more! Earlier in June, Venus and Jupiter will have a close meeting in the sky. Around June 9, they’ll appear right next to each other after sunset. Then from June 11 to 15, Mercury joins the party, making a line of three planets low in the west. These gatherings happen because all planets travel along the same path in our sky, called the ecliptic. Sometimes they bunch up from our view on Earth. Venus is super easy to spot because it’s so bright. Jupiter is bright too, but Mercury is trickier—it’s low and faint. A clear view of the horizon helps. One big safety tip: if you try to see the Moon cover Venus during the day, never point binoculars or a telescope near the Sun. It can hurt your eyes badly. June also brings the summer solstice, the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. And later at night, look for the Summer Triangle—three bright stars named Vega, Altair, and Deneb. It’s a great month to look up!
why_it_matters: Seeing these events shows that our sky is like a giant clock, and you can be part of it just by looking up—no special equipment needed.

background_read: In ancient times, people often saw occultations as omens, but today we know they happen because the Moon moves in front of distant objects.
The ecliptic is the invisible path in the sky where the Sun, Moon, and planets all travel, making close meetings possible.
The Summer Triangle—formed by the bright stars Vega, Altair, and Deneb—shines in summer and is a guide for stargazers.
Article_Structure: WHO: People in parts of the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Venezuela.
WHAT: Venus will vanish behind the Moon (a lunar occultation) and planets will gather close together in the evening sky.
WHERE: In the western sky after sunset, low toward the horizon.
WHY: Because all planets orbit along the same ecliptic path, causing them to bunch up from our viewpoint on Earth.

perspectives.description: They find it thrilling to watch a rare celestial hide-and-seek that costs nothing to view.
They emphasize that viewing the Sun directly, especially with binoculars, can cause permanent eye damage, so caution is crucial.
They see these alignments as normal but love sharing the science behind the patterns.
